sections.title: Policy and access to the centre
sections.text: Oisterwijk, a small town in Noord-Brabant with a well-known nature area on its doorstep, is not a free-parking town: the centre and the station area are paid. The council adopted the parking tax ordinance for 2026 on 11 December 2025. In the centre zone it charges 0.25 euro for the first quarter-hour, 0.55 euro for each of the second and third, 0.80 euro for the fourth and then 2.40 euros an hour from the second hour; in the other zone, which covers marked streets and car parks, it charges 1.55 euros an hour with a day ticket of 6.20 euros [0]. Paid hours run Monday to Thursday from 09:00 to 18:00, Friday until 21:00 and Saturday until 17:00, and parking is free on Sundays and outside those hours [1]. A first resident permit costs 49.65 euros without a private space and 114.00 euros with one, and the fine is 76.00 euros with no remission [2]. Disabled card holders on marked bays and electric vehicles that are charging are exempt [3]. The rates are the same as in 2024 and 2025, when the centre rate was last raised from 2.30 to 2.40 euros [4]. Long-stay parkers push into the streets around the paid centre, so the town runs disc zones with a free licence-plate exemption for residents and businesses [7], added a two-hour disc zone in the Schoolstraat in 2021 [10] and in September 2025 made four bays on the Moergestelseweg a 30-minute disc zone for short visits [8].

sections.title: Parking developments
sections.text: The visible changes are in charging. On 1 October 2026 the college published a traffic decision reserving two bays at each of 11 new charge points, nine chosen where existing chargers are heavily used and one location, Sportlaan 22, as a strategic site; it rests on a Vattenfall InCharge contract held by the provinces of Noord-Brabant and Limburg [15]. A pilot with chargers without reserved bays, run from 1 August 2026, is reported by two automatically composed press articles that disagree on its end date and locations, and we found no official source, so we treat it as unconfirmed [14]. For new housing, the 2016 parking-standards note sets standards by area and a rate table for a mobility fund that applies only if the council sets one up, at 5,000 euros per space in the centre; it is an old document [9]. A 2022 study found that visitors rated parking by car in the centre at 7.0 out of 10, below Moergestel and Haaren at 8.1, and estimated about 416,000 visits a year to the Oisterwijkse Bossen en Vennen; it recommends analysing peak-time bottlenecks, which is a recommendation and not a decision [11][12].

sections.title: Operators, positioning and utilisation
sections.text:
The map of the 2026 designation decision shows eight signed paid car parks, all at 1.55 euros an hour: Stationsplein, Gemullehoekenweg (two lots), Spoorlaan-Jumbo, Marktpad, Burg. Verwielstraat, Vloeiweg-AH and Vloeiweg-Mevio. The Spoorlaan along the station is in the same zone, but the map names no park-and-ride lot and gives no space counts [5]. In 2019 the same map showed J. Lenartzstraat in place of the later Vloeiweg-Mevio, with the centre rate at 2.00 euros an hour, 20 percent lower [6]. We found no source on who operates the car parks or on station parking, because the municipal site was offline when we read it.

Our data cover a car park listed as P+R Spoorlaan, with 137 spaces, for about 61 days since 22 August 2026. Occupancy averaged about 11% on weekdays and 8% at weekends, with a peak of 61% around midday on a Sunday. We could not match it to any of the eight car parks on the municipal map, so we cannot say whether it is one of the paid sites.
